//name: The extension ID is publisher.name, so this pair reads `ffwf.tau-code`. It is not the npm scope -- an extension name may not contain `@` or `/`. The `tau-code.*` setting and command IDs below are a third namespace again, and are deliberately unchanged: renaming them would silently drop a user's settings.
name: tau-code
//displayName: A FOURTH namespace, and the only global one: `name` is scoped by publisher, so `ffwf.tau-code` is ours as soon as we own `ffwf`, but a display name is unique across the entire Marketplace and no publisher prefix applies. `tau` was refused as taken. This one matches every other identifier here -- the repository, the extension name, the .vsix. Open VSX enforces no such rule.
description: Run a tau agent inside VS Code or VSCodium.
//private: `private` stops an accidental `npm publish`. It does not stop a marketplace publish: scripts/publish-extension.sh publishes the built .vsix by path, and vsce reads the manifest out of the archive rather than off disk.
//capabilities: Both were absent, which is not the same as neutral: an undeclared extension is disabled in a Restricted Mode workspace with no sentence saying so. Opening an untrusted folder in VS Code proper therefore showed no tau icon, no command, and nothing in the log -- the extension was never loaded, and the reader had no way to learn that trust was the reason. Declaring `false` changes no behaviour; it supplies the explanation VS Code shows in the trust UI, which is the whole defect.

untrustedWorkspaces.description: tau runs shell commands and edits files in the open folder, on instructions from a model that read that folder. There is no reduced mode that is still an agent, so this asks for trust rather than pretending to work without it.

virtualWorkspaces.description: tau is a local process with a working directory. A workspace served from a remote index has no filesystem to be that directory.

//packaging: What lands in the .vsix is controlled by .vscodeignore. vsce refuses to accept both that and a `files` property, so there is no `files` here.
//extensionKind: `workspace` so the agent's tools run where the code is -- over SSH, in WSL, in a devcontainer -- rather than on the laptop. The webview always renders locally regardless, which is the split a standalone web app cannot reproduce.
//activationEvents: One entry, and it is the one VS Code cannot infer. Commands and views are inferred from `contributes` below, so this stayed empty and looked finished. A webview PANEL has no contribution point -- its viewType exists only in code -- so a reopened window restores the `tau` tab, finds no extension awake to deserialize it, and leaves it blank until something else happens to activate us. The serializer in extension.ts was already written for this; without the line it was never called.

enumDescriptions: The bundled runtime extension when it is installed, otherwise tau on PATH.
Only the bundled runtime extension. Refuses to start when it is absent, rather than running a different tau.
Only tau on PATH, or whatever tau-code.binary names. The runtime extension is ignored even if installed.
tau-code.runtime.markdownDescription:
Which tau to run when more than one is available.

`ffwf.tau-runtime` is a separate, optional extension that ships its own CPython with tau installed into it. When it and a system tau are both present, this decides — and if the two are different versions, the panel says so rather than picking quietly.

A `tau-code.binary` you have set explicitly, or `TAU_BIN`, wins over all three: naming a path is an instruction, and a path that does not work is an error rather than a reason to run something else.

tau-code.binary.markdownDescription:
Path to tau's console script. A bare name is looked up on PATH.

Leave it at `tau` to let `tau-code.runtime` decide. Setting it to anything else overrides that setting entirely, including the bundled runtime.

tau-code.model.description: Passed to tau as --model. Empty uses tau's own configured default.

tau-code.provider.description: Passed to tau as --provider. Empty uses tau's own configured default.

tau-code.sessionDir.markdownDescription:
Where session logs are written (`--session-dir`).

Empty uses tau's default for RPC hosts: a private `<tmp>/.tau-<uid>/sessions`, so this extension does not fill the session list you see in the TUI. **Those sessions do not survive a reboot on a system that clears its temp directory.**

Set this to `~/.tau/sessions` to share one store with the tau TUI and `tau -p`. The two are then fully interchangeable in both directions: this extension can resume a session the TUI wrote, and the TUI's `--continue` resumes one written here.

//package: --no-dependencies because esbuild bundles everything into dist/extension.js: without it vsce walks the workspace-hoisted ../../node_modules and fails on a path outside the extension.
//dependencies: The three @ffwf/* entries are workspace siblings, unpublished by design, so they are ranged `*` rather than pinned -- see `//internal-deps` in the root package.json. Nothing resolves them at install time for a user anyway: esbuild bundles them into dist/extension.js and the .vsix is built --no-dependencies.
